opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to fairness that people can actually see. Today, if you publish something on the web, the deal is murky. Your content gets crawled, it ends up inside a model or gets pulled into an answer, and you don't really know how much it mattered or whether you'll ever see anything for it. That uncertainty is why so many publishers are putting up walls. Everyone is defensive because nobody trusts the accounting.

Shapley values are interesting because they come from cooperative game theory, and they answer a very specific question: if a group of contributors together produced some value, how much of that value is attributable to each one? They have properties people intuitively agree with. If you contributed nothing to an outcome, you get nothing. If two sources contributed the same thing, they get the same share. And the shares add up to the whole. You don't have to be a mathematician to feel that this is a reasonable way to split things.

In an agentic world, that matters a lot. When an agent is doing a task on someone's behalf, it might touch dozens of sources to produce one answer. Some were essential, some were redundant, some were noise. A Shapley-style approach lets you pay according to marginal contribution to that specific answer, rather than for raw access or volume. A small, specialized publisher with one uniquely valuable piece of information can be rewarded fairly, even next to a giant site. That's what pulls in the long tail. It's not just a deal for the ten biggest media companies.

It works for the buyer side too. If you're building agents, you want access to the best information on the open web, and you don't want to negotiate a thousand bilateral licenses. A market with a principled, transparent way of pricing contribution means you pay for what actually helped, and you get access to content that would otherwise be locked away.

To be clear, exact Shapley computation is expensive, so in practice you approximate it, and the details of measurement really matter. But the principle gives both sides a reason to show up: creators get paid for value rather than clicks, and agent builders get a scalable, defensible way to use the web. When the incentives line up like that, I think broad participation follows. The web was built on an implicit bargain, and this is a way of making a new bargain explicit for the agent era.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the starting point is that the current web economy for content is broken for the agentic era. The old deal was simple: you put content online, search engines sent you traffic, and you monetized that traffic through ads or subscriptions. Agents break that deal. An agent reads your page, synthesizes an answer, and the user never visits you. So the publisher gets nothing, and over time the incentive to produce good content erodes, which is bad for everyone, including the agent builders who depend on that content.

So why Shapley specifically? Because the hard problem isn't willingness to pay. It's attribution. When an agent answers a question, it might have drawn on twenty sources, and the value of each one depends on what else was in the mix. A single source might be worthless on its own but decisive in combination with another. Shapley values are the one principled way to handle exactly that: you ask, across all the possible subsets of sources, what did this source contribute on the margin? It's the only allocation that's efficient, symmetric, and gives zero to content that added nothing. That fairness property turns out to matter enormously for participation, because people will join a market they believe is fair even when the individual payouts are small.

And I think that's the key to broad participation. Three things have to be true. First, the publisher side has to believe they're not being gamed, that a big brand isn't getting paid just for being big. Shapley gives you that, because contribution is measured by marginal value, not by traffic or reputation. Second, the long tail has to see money. Under a traffic model, the long tail got crumbs. Under a contribution model, a niche forum post that resolves a specific question can be the most valuable input to that answer, and it gets paid accordingly. That brings in participants who were never going to win the SEO game. Third, the agent builders have to want it, and they do, because the alternative is either scraping with legal exposure or negotiating bespoke licensing deals with a few hundred large publishers, which structurally starves the rest of the web.

Now, the honest caveat is that exact Shapley is computationally brutal. You can't enumerate every subset. So in practice you're using sampling and approximation, and the market participants have to trust the approximation. That's a real engineering and governance challenge. But I'd argue we've already learned how to do this in ad markets, where nobody computes the theoretically perfect auction either, yet trillions of dollars flow through them because the mechanism is transparent enough and the incentives are roughly aligned.

So my belief comes down to this: participation follows fairness plus liquidity. Shapley gives you a credible fairness story. Agents give you the liquidity, because they're going to consume orders of magnitude more content than humans ever clicked on. Put those together and you have a market where a lot of people, including people who've been shut out of the current web economy, have a reason to show up.

astra-6.text:
I think the appeal is that you can reward contribution without requiring everyone to negotiate a separate deal. With a Shapley-based approach, the question is: how much does this piece of content add to the value an agent delivers, taking into account the other content available? That gives you a principled starting point for sharing the value created.

For a publisher, that creates a reason to make useful content available. For an agent developer, it creates a way to access that content and pay in proportion to its contribution. And it leaves room for smaller creators: a niche source could be very valuable for a particular task even if it doesn’t have a large audience.

But the mechanism alone isn’t enough. Participation has to be easy, the measurement has to be credible, and the economics have to work for both sides. If you can deliver those things, there’s a plausible path to broad participation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the appeal is that you don’t have to agree in advance on what every piece of content is worth. A Shapley-based approach gives you a principle for sharing the value: how much did a particular source contribute to the result, taking into account the other sources available?

That can make participation attractive on both sides. Publishers have a reason to make useful content available because they can be compensated for its contribution. AI agents have a reason to participate because they get access to content that improves their answers, with payment tied to the value it provides.

But the allocation rule alone isn’t enough. You need a practical way to estimate contributions, payments people can understand and trust, and very little friction to join. If you can deliver those things, participation can reinforce itself: more useful content attracts more agents, and more demand attracts more content.
